questions.prompt: During FGCP failover, what state lets the new primary continue an eligible TCP flow?

options.text: The secondary receives TCP session-table updates from the primary.
options.feedback: Those updates let the new primary recognize an existing flow and continue its last known state.

options.text: Only the running configuration is copied after each policy install.
options.feedback: Configuration synchronization is separate; identical policy configuration does not preserve live session entries.

options.text: VPN control sessions are restarted automatically by the new primary.
options.feedback: Cluster-terminated VPN sessions generally reconnect; they are not ordinary transit sessions.

options.text: Every proxy-inspected flow is recreated with full inspection state.
options.feedback: Proxy-based inspection sessions are not supported for session pickup, and flow-based sessions have an inspection caveat.

questions.prompt: A TCP session crosses an FGCP cluster using proxy-based security profiles. What should the engineer expect after failover?

options.text: The new primary resumes the proxy session with full inspection state.
options.feedback: That overstates the feature; proxy-based inspected sessions are outside the supported session-pickup boundary.

options.text: Proxy-based inspection sessions are not supported for session pickup.
options.feedback: Fortinet documents that proxy-based security-profile sessions do not fail over through session pickup.

options.text: The new primary synchronizes the proxy cache before promotion.
options.feedback: Session pickup synchronizes eligible session state, not a complete proxy inspection context.

options.text: The old primary transfers its application proxy process to the secondary.
options.feedback: FGCP does not migrate a running proxy process as part of session pickup.

questions.prompt: Which setting adds UDP and ICMP state synchronization to session pickup?

options.text: Enable session-pickup-delay to synchronize every UDP session.
options.feedback: The delay option is about eligible TCP synchronization on supported platforms, not connectionless protocols.

options.text: Enable session-sync-dev to create connectionless session entries.
options.feedback: That selects a synchronization interface; it does not enable connectionless session pickup.

options.text: Enable session-pickup-connectionless to synchronize UDP and ICMP sessions.
options.feedback: The connectionless option extends synchronization to UDP and ICMP; it should be enabled only when required.

options.text: Enable session-pickup-expectation to copy all UDP sessions.
options.feedback: Expectation synchronization concerns helper-created related sessions and is not the UDP/ICMP switch.

questions.prompt: Why can HA heartbeat utilization rise sharply during failover or member rejoin?

options.text: The cluster replays every historical traffic log across heartbeat links.
options.feedback: Traffic logs are not the session synchronization payload; the load comes from session state.

options.text: The secondary downloads all firmware packages during promotion.
options.feedback: Firmware image transfer is not the normal session-pickup process during failover.

options.text: The cluster repeats every FortiGuard rating lookup during election.
options.feedback: Rating lookups are not the reason session synchronization traffic surges on heartbeat links.

options.text: Failover can trigger synchronization of the full session table.
options.feedback: The primary must bring the joining or promoted member's session state up to date, creating a burst.

questions.prompt: Which IPS template objects are global versus VDOM-scoped in FortiManager?

options.text: IPS Global is global; System IPS and IPS Settings are VDOM-scoped.
options.feedback: FortiManager explicitly separates global IPS configuration from the two VDOM-based objects.

options.text: All three IPS objects are copied only to the root VDOM.
options.feedback: System IPS and IPS Settings are VDOM-scoped, while IPS Global is global.

options.text: System IPS is global; IPS Global belongs to each VDOM.
options.feedback: This reverses the documented scopes of the three IPS objects.

options.text: IPS Settings is global; the other objects are VDOM-scoped.
options.feedback: IPS Settings is VDOM-based, and IPS Global is the global object.

questions.prompt: A template is assigned to the root VDOM. Which object scope is copied?

options.text: System IPS and IPS Settings are copied to every VDOM.
options.feedback: Those are VDOM-based objects and are not copied to root/mgmt by this operation.

options.text: Only IPS Global is copied to root or mgmt.
options.feedback: The 7.6.6 guide explicitly limits root/mgmt targets to the global IPS object.

options.text: All objects are copied, but hidden in the device database.
options.feedback: The guide says only IPS Global is copied; this is not a visibility issue.

options.text: No IPS objects are copied until a policy package is installed.
options.feedback: The root/mgmt exception still copies IPS Global when the template is applied.

questions.prompt: A VDOM IPS setting is missing after assignment. What should be checked first?

options.text: Rebuild the IPS signature database on the FortiGate.
options.feedback: Signature database health does not explain a missing VDOM-scoped template object.

options.text: Change the ADOM version without checking the target.
options.feedback: Version compatibility may matter, but the target VDOM and generated diff are the first checks.

options.text: Review the target VDOM and install diff before assuming deployment.
options.feedback: The VDOM target controls which scoped objects are applicable; the diff shows what FortiManager will install.

options.text: Delete the device group and re-add the same FortiGate.
options.feedback: Recreating the group does not correct an incorrect VDOM target or object scope.

questions.prompt: A restricted IPS administrator cannot see IPS Templates. What is the likely cause?

options.text: The FortiGate lacks an IPS license for this device.
options.feedback: Device licensing does not determine whether the FortiManager administrator menu is visible.

options.text: The ADOM is automatically locked by the IPS engine.
options.feedback: An ADOM lock is not the documented prerequisite for the restricted IPS menu.

options.text: The template can only be edited from the FortiGate CLI.
options.feedback: FortiManager provides a dedicated IPS Templates view for restricted administrators.

options.text: The administrator profile lacks the IPS Templates permission.
options.feedback: FortiManager exposes the menu to an IPS-restricted administrator when the relevant permission is granted.

questions.prompt: Which Asset Identity Center source is disabled by default and must be enabled?

options.text: EMS Connector identification is disabled until explicitly enabled.
options.feedback: FortiAnalyzer documents EMS Connector identity identification as disabled by default.

options.text: FortiGate log identification is disabled for every ADOM.
options.feedback: FortiGate log identification is enabled by default for all devices and subnets.

options.text: FortiClient log identification is disabled for every device.
options.feedback: FortiClient log identification is enabled by default for all devices.

options.text: FortiNAC log identification is disabled for every device.
options.feedback: FortiNAC log identification is enabled by default for all devices.

questions.prompt: A broad source rule is ON, but one device contributes no identities. Why?

options.text: The identity engine ignores devices with active sessions.
options.feedback: Session activity is not the documented precedence mechanism for Asset Identity data sources.

options.text: Device-specific source rules override broad all-device rules.
options.feedback: An individual-device rule has higher priority than an all-devices rule and can exclude that device.

options.text: The device must be moved into the root ADOM.
options.feedback: The relevant control is per-ADOM source selection, not a universal root-ADOM requirement.

options.text: FortiAnalyzer only imports identities from EMS connectors.
options.feedback: The feature supports multiple log sources, including FortiGate, FortiClient, FortiMail, FortiWeb, and FortiNAC.

questions.prompt: Where is endpoint and end-user data-source configuration scoped?

options.text: It is global across every ADOM on the appliance.
options.feedback: The guide explicitly makes the configuration per ADOM.

options.text: It is scoped to the administrator's user group only.
options.feedback: User permissions govern access, but the source selection is associated with an ADOM.

options.text: Data-source configuration is scoped to the selected ADOM.
options.feedback: The FortiAnalyzer 8.0 guide states that data-source modification is configured per ADOM.

options.text: It is stored only in the FortiGate device database.
options.feedback: The source rules are configured in FortiAnalyzer Fabric View, not on each FortiGate.

questions.prompt: What sequence is required to populate EMS vulnerability data in Asset Identity Center?

options.text: Enable the report template, then wait for FortiGate logs.
options.feedback: A report template alone does not call the EMS API or create Fabric logs.

options.text: Create a FortiGate event handler, then add an ADOM.
options.feedback: The EMS workflow uses a connector and sequence playbook, not a FortiGate event handler.

options.text: Add EMS as a source before authorizing the device.
options.feedback: The documented process authorizes EMS and creates its connector before source selection.

options.text: Authorize EMS, create connector, enable playbook, then add source.
options.feedback: The documented pipeline needs an authorized EMS device, connector, sequence playbook, and enabled EMS data source.

questions.prompt: What is the documented default packet sample rate for FortiSwitch flow export?

options.text: The default sample rate is one packet in 512.
options.feedback: FortiSwitch flow export uses a default rate of one sampled packet per 512 packets.

options.text: The default sample rate is one packet in 64.
options.feedback: That is a possible configured rate, not the documented default.

options.text: The default sample rate is one packet in 1024.
options.feedback: That is not the documented default for the feature.

options.text: The default sample rate is every packet on each port.
options.feedback: Sampling is enabled with a rate; the default is not full packet capture.

questions.prompt: How does NetFlow v5 derive the exported sample-rate value?

options.text: It derives the rate from the collector's template interval.
options.feedback: Template refresh is separate from the sample-rate value encoded in NetFlow v5.

options.text: NetFlow v5 derives sampling rate from the lowest enabled port.
options.feedback: Fortinet notes that v5 derives the sample rate from the lowest-numbered port with sampling enabled.

options.text: It averages all configured port rates before export.
options.feedback: The documented behavior uses the lowest port number, not an average.

options.text: It reads the rate from the switch serial number.
options.feedback: The serial number is not the source of the NetFlow v5 sample-rate field.

questions.prompt: Which fields are included when FortiSwitch flow tracking uses VLAN level?

options.text: VLAN level exports only source and destination MAC addresses.
options.feedback: That is a Layer-2 identity view, not the VLAN-level IP flow field set.

options.text: VLAN level exports only IP addresses and interface indexes.
options.feedback: The VLAN level also includes ports, protocol, TOS, and VLAN ID.

options.text: VLAN level exports IPs, ports, protocol, and VLAN.
options.feedback: The VLAN level includes source/destination IPs, ports, protocol, and VLAN information.

options.text: VLAN level exports payload bytes from every sampled packet.
options.feedback: Flow export records summarize headers and counters; they do not export packet payloads.

questions.prompt: Why must a collector receive flow templates as well as flowsets?

options.text: Templates contain the switch's complete running configuration.
options.feedback: Flow templates describe exported record structure, not the switch configuration.

options.text: Templates authenticate the collector using the switch serial number.
options.feedback: Template packets are for record decoding, not collector authentication.

options.text: Templates replace sampling and make packet inspection unnecessary.
options.feedback: Sampling still creates the flow records; templates only describe their structure.

options.text: Templates define flow fields and refresh every five minutes.
options.feedback: The collector needs the template to decode the fields carried in subsequent flowsets.

questions.prompt: When both Dynamic VLAN and VLAN pooling are enabled, which assignment wins?

options.text: Tunnel-Private-Group-ID takes precedence over the VLAN pool.
options.feedback: FortiOS 8.0 uses the VLAN returned in the RADIUS Access-Accept when present.

options.text: The FortiAP group pool always overrides the RADIUS attribute.
options.feedback: The documented precedence is the opposite: the RADIUS VLAN wins.

options.text: The SSID static VLAN always overrides both dynamic methods.
options.feedback: The static VLAN is not the preferred result when a valid RADIUS VLAN is returned.

options.text: The controller randomly chooses between the two VLAN sources.
options.feedback: There is a defined priority order, not a random selection.

questions.prompt: What happens when the RADIUS Access-Accept has no Tunnel-Private-Group-ID?

options.text: The client is rejected even though RADIUS authentication succeeded.
options.feedback: The documented fallback allows an authenticated client to receive a pool VLAN.

options.text: The AP group's configured pool supplies the fallback VLAN.
options.feedback: FortiOS 8.0 falls back to the local VLAN pool based on the connected FortiAP group.

options.text: The controller reuses the previous user's VLAN assignment.
options.feedback: The fallback is based on the AP's configured pool, not another user's session.

options.text: The controller selects the first VLAN interface alphabetically.
options.feedback: The configured VLAN pool and FortiAP group determine the fallback.

questions.prompt: Which RADIUS tunnel attributes identify a VLAN assignment?

options.text: Tunnel-Type 6, Tunnel-Medium-Type 13, and group ID 100.
options.feedback: The first two values are reversed; the standard values are 13 and 6.

options.text: Calling-Station-Id 13, NAS-Port 6, and group ID 100.
options.feedback: Those are not the three RADIUS tunnel attributes used for VLAN assignment.

options.text: Tunnel-Type 13, Tunnel-Medium-Type 6, and group ID 100.
options.feedback: The standard values identify VLAN over IEEE 802 and carry the VLAN ID.

options.text: Tunnel-Type 100, Tunnel-Medium-Type 13, and group ID 6.
options.feedback: The VLAN ID belongs in Tunnel-Private-Group-ID, not in the medium field.

questions.prompt: A station shows the intended VLAN but receives no DHCP lease. What is missing?

options.text: The RADIUS server must send the VLAN attribute twice.
options.feedback: A repeated attribute does not create the missing VLAN interface or DHCP service.

options.text: The AP must be rebooted after every successful authentication.
options.feedback: A reboot is not a substitute for the required VLAN and DHCP configuration.

options.text: The client must authenticate using a second SSID.
options.feedback: The station already has the intended VLAN; investigate Layer-2 and Layer-3 services.

options.text: Correct VLAN selection does not create DHCP or firewall policy.
options.feedback: The VLAN must also exist on the data path with addressing, DHCP, and policy.

questions.prompt: Which inputs can Persistent Agent use to discover its FortiNAC server?

options.text: Persistent Agent checks SRV records and local server settings.
options.feedback: The documented order includes DNS SRV, registry/preferences/configuration, and last-connected/home/allowed server values.

options.text: Persistent Agent uses only the captive portal URL.
options.feedback: Externally deployed agents can use DNS and local settings without portal download.

options.text: Persistent Agent queries only an LDAP service record.
options.feedback: The documented service names are Bradford Agent SRV records, not an LDAP lookup.

options.text: Persistent Agent discovers the server from switch LLDP neighbors.
options.feedback: LLDP topology is not the Persistent Agent server-discovery mechanism.

questions.prompt: Which ports are documented for Persistent Agent communication and upgrades?

options.text: Persistent Agent uses TCP 1812; TCP 1813 handles upgrades.
options.feedback: Those are common RADIUS ports, not the Persistent Agent ports.

options.text: Persistent Agent uses TCP 4568; TCP 80 handles upgrades.
options.feedback: The FortiNAC guide lists TCP 4568 for communication and TCP 80 for upgrades.

options.text: Persistent Agent uses TCP 443 only for all operations.
options.feedback: TLS is used, but the documented Persistent Agent ports include 4568 and 80.

options.text: Persistent Agent uses UDP 161; TCP 22 handles upgrades.
options.feedback: Those are SNMP and SSH ports, not the documented agent ports.

questions.prompt: DNS resolves, but the agent's TLS connection still fails. What should be checked?

options.text: The FortiNAC database must be rebuilt before another scan.
options.feedback: A database rebuild does not correct a DNS name/certificate identity mismatch.

options.text: The endpoint must use the same VLAN as the server.
options.feedback: VLAN placement may affect reachability, but it does not correct TLS name validation.

options.text: The discovered server name must match its certificate target.
options.feedback: Fortinet requires the Application Server name used by the agent to match the certificate target for that agent type.

options.text: The endpoint must permanently disable certificate checks for agents.
options.feedback: Disabling security is not the recommended fix; correct the name and certificate target for that agent.

questions.prompt: How does the Passive Agent obtain its Application Server list?

options.text: Passive Agent uses the _bradfordagent SRV record first.
options.feedback: That SRV discovery sequence is documented for Persistent Agent, not Passive Agent.

options.text: Passive Agent reads the FortiAP group VLAN pool.
options.feedback: Wireless VLAN configuration is unrelated to agent server discovery.

options.text: Passive Agent obtains its server from an EAP-TLS certificate.
options.feedback: The server list comes from the registry entry used by the logon script.

options.text: Passive Agent reads ServerURL from the host registry.
options.feedback: The Passive Agent is launched by a logon script that reads the registry ServerURL list.

questions.prompt: A replacement switch reuses the old management IP and polling fails. What is likely stale?

options.text: The cached engine ID belongs to the replaced device.
options.feedback: FortiNAC-F documents clearing the cached engine ID after device replacement or IP reuse.

options.text: The FortiNAC license still references the old switch serial.
options.feedback: The documented recovery is to clear the SNMP engine ID cache, not change licensing.

options.text: The SNMPv3 username is always locked after an IP change.
options.feedback: An IP change does not inherently lock the SNMPv3 username.

options.text: The CLI enable password is stored in the SNMP engine cache.
options.feedback: CLI credentials are separate from the SNMPv3 engine ID cache.

questions.prompt: Which tool clears the cached engine ID when the device is not added?

options.text: ResetSNMPUser -ip 192.0.2.25 recreates the user account.
options.feedback: That is not the documented cache-clear tool and would change the wrong object.

options.text: ClearEngineID -ip 192.0.2.25 clears the cached engine ID.
options.feedback: The FortiNAC-F device-properties guide documents the ClearEngineID tool with the device IP.

options.text: ClearCredential -serial 192.0.2.25 resets all passwords.
options.feedback: The documented tool targets the engine ID by IP, not all credentials.

options.text: RefreshDevice -force 192.0.2.25 deletes the inventory entry.
options.feedback: Refreshing or deleting the device is not the documented engine-ID cache operation.

questions.prompt: Which settings are required for SNMPv3 AuthPriv polling?

options.text: Only a community string and an SNMPv2 view are required.
options.feedback: Community strings belong to SNMPv1/v2c, not SNMPv3 AuthPriv.

options.text: Only a CLI username and SSH private key are required.
options.feedback: CLI access is separate from SNMPv3 authentication and privacy.

options.text: SNMPv3 AuthPriv requires authentication and privacy credentials for polling.
options.feedback: AuthPriv uses an authentication protocol/password and a privacy protocol/password.

options.text: Only an engine ID and read-only password are required.
options.feedback: The engine ID is part of USM processing, but AuthPriv also needs configured auth and privacy credentials.

questions.prompt: What does Validate Credentials prove, and what does it not clear?

options.text: It clears the engine ID and changes the SNMP username.
options.feedback: The UI provides a separate Clear Cached Engine ID action.

options.text: It proves VLAN enforcement works on every switch port.
options.feedback: Credential validation tests management access, not endpoint VLAN enforcement.

options.text: It resets the device and removes all polling history.
options.feedback: The validation action is a test, not a destructive device reset.

options.text: Credential validation tests access but does not clear engine identity.
options.feedback: The button tests CLI/SNMP credentials; cache clearing is a separate operation.

questions.prompt: What does selecting MAC Device for the client certificate CN accomplish?

options.text: MAC Device places the registered endpoint MAC in certificate CN.
options.feedback: The SmartConnect profile can use a registered MAC device as the client certificate CN.

options.text: It copies the RADIUS shared secret into the certificate subject.
options.feedback: The CN is an identity value, not a RADIUS shared secret.

options.text: It places the user's email address in the certificate issuer field.
options.feedback: The option selects a MAC device for the subject CN, not an issuer field.

options.text: It disables endpoint registration and accepts any certificate by default.
options.feedback: Device registration is part of the binding workflow; the option does not bypass certificate checks.

questions.prompt: When MAC-to-CN verification is enabled, what does RADIUS compare?

options.text: RADIUS compares the switch serial number with the issuer name.
options.feedback: The comparison is between endpoint MAC and certificate CN.

options.text: RADIUS compares the request's endpoint MAC with certificate CN.
options.feedback: The policy compares the endpoint MAC supplied by the RADIUS client with the certificate subject CN.

options.text: RADIUS compares the user password with the certificate thumbprint.
options.feedback: EAP-TLS does not compare a password to the certificate thumbprint.

options.text: RADIUS compares the AP name with the certificate validity date.
options.feedback: Neither AP name nor certificate date is the MAC-to-CN check.

questions.prompt: A user has no registered MAC devices. What happens to MAC-bound SmartConnect selection?

options.text: The profile silently uses the username as the MAC address.
options.feedback: The MAC Device option requires a registered device; it does not invent a MAC.

options.text: FortiAuthenticator accepts any endpoint and skips the RADIUS policy.
options.feedback: The feature is designed to bind the endpoint identity, not bypass policy.

options.text: No registered MAC device prevents selecting a MAC-bound certificate.
options.feedback: The portal cannot offer a device-bound certificate choice when the user has no registered MAC device.

options.text: The RADIUS client assigns a random VLAN as the certificate CN.
options.feedback: VLAN assignment and certificate subject construction are separate mechanisms.

questions.prompt: A trusted certificate is rejected by the MAC-to-CN check. What distinction matters?

options.text: A valid certificate automatically overrides every RADIUS policy check.
options.feedback: The policy can perform additional device authorization after certificate validation.

options.text: A valid certificate proves the endpoint's current switch port.
options.feedback: The certificate chain does not identify the current physical switch port.

options.text: A valid certificate means Calling-Station-Id is ignored.
options.feedback: The MAC-to-CN feature specifically uses the endpoint MAC supplied by the RADIUS client.

options.text: Certificate-chain validation proves trust, not endpoint-to-MAC binding.
options.feedback: A trusted issuer does not prove that the presenting endpoint matches the registered MAC in the CN.

questions.prompt: What does Access Authentication require before a user accesses a secret?

options.text: Access Authentication requires fresh user authentication before secret access.
options.feedback: The control adds a reauthentication gate before protected secret operations are available.

options.text: An approver must approve every secret launch request.
options.feedback: That is the separate Requires Approval to Launch Secret control.

options.text: The user must check out the secret exclusively.
options.feedback: Checkout is a separate control that grants exclusive use for a limited time.

options.text: The secret password must rotate before each access.
options.feedback: Password changing is separate from the Access Authentication gate.

questions.prompt: What is the default validity duration and allowed range?

options.text: The default is 30 minutes; valid values range 5–60.
options.feedback: Those values are not the documented Access Authentication duration.

options.text: The default is 60 minutes; valid values range 0–180.
options.feedback: FortiPAM documents a 60-minute default and a zero-to-180-minute range.

options.text: The default is 120 minutes; valid values range 30–240.
options.feedback: The documented default and range are 60 and 0–180.

options.text: The default is 15 minutes; valid values range 1–90.
options.feedback: Those values are not the documented Access Authentication duration.

questions.prompt: What does a zero-minute Access Authentication duration mean?

options.text: Zero disables authentication and permanently trusts the user.
options.feedback: Zero is not a bypass; it creates the most restrictive short-lived use.

options.text: Zero grants an unlimited session until the user logs out.
options.feedback: The documented behavior is short-lived, not unlimited.

options.text: Zero minutes creates short-lived immediate-use authorization for one secret.
options.feedback: FortiPAM describes zero as short-lived authorization for immediate use, effectively one secret.

options.text: Zero requires two administrators to approve each secret access.
options.feedback: Approval profiles are separate from the duration of Access Authentication.

questions.prompt: What is the default state of Bypass For Owners?

options.text: Owner bypass is enabled for every secret by default.
options.feedback: The guide lists the default as disabled.

options.text: Owner bypass applies only to session recording controls.
options.feedback: It is an Access Authentication exception for secret owners.

options.text: Owner bypass is mandatory whenever a folder policy exists.
options.feedback: Folder policy can protect settings, but owner bypass remains a separate optional setting.

options.text: Owner bypass is disabled by default and should be documented.
options.feedback: FortiPAM defaults this exception to disabled; enabling it should be deliberate.

questions.prompt: Which data does FortiSIEM Manager retain locally?

options.text: Manager stores incidents and latest license, not raw events.
options.feedback: The Manager stores incidents and latest license information in PostgreSQL, plus one day of health data; raw events remain on instances.

options.text: Manager stores every raw event from every registered instance.
options.feedback: The guide explicitly says raw events are not stored in the Manager.

options.text: Manager stores only raw events and discards incident metadata.
options.feedback: Incident metadata is stored centrally and forwarded near real time.

options.text: Manager stores complete event databases for one year.
options.feedback: The Manager is not a central event database and has no such documented retention.

questions.prompt: Where are raw triggering events retrieved when an analyst opens an incident?

options.text: They are reconstructed from the Manager's health database.
options.feedback: Health metadata is not a substitute for the source event records.

options.text: Raw triggering events are fetched from the source instance.
options.feedback: The Manager fetches raw events on demand from the FortiSIEM instance where the incident occurred.

options.text: They are downloaded from the FortiManager policy package.
options.feedback: FortiManager policy packages are unrelated to FortiSIEM event retrieval.

options.text: They are fetched from the FortiSASE tunnel logs.
options.feedback: The incident's originating FortiSIEM instance is the documented raw-event source.

questions.prompt: What are the documented health and license forwarding intervals?

options.text: Health arrives hourly; license data arrives every minute.
options.feedback: This reverses the documented cadences.

options.text: Both health and license data arrive every five minutes.
options.feedback: The documented intervals are one minute and one hour.

options.text: Health arrives every minute; license data arrives hourly.
options.feedback: The Manager receives health once per minute and license information once per hour.

options.text: Health arrives every thirty seconds; license data arrives daily.
options.feedback: Those intervals are not the documented Manager forwarding cadence.

questions.prompt: Which upgrade order is required for a Manager deployment?

options.text: Upgrade every Supervisor first, then upgrade the Manager.
options.feedback: The documented order is the opposite.

options.text: Upgrade all Collectors first, then register a new Manager.
options.feedback: The Manager is upgraded before the registered instances.

options.text: Upgrade the Manager only after all instances are upgraded.
options.feedback: That reverses the explicit Fortinet upgrade requirement.

options.text: Upgrade FortiSIEM Manager before upgrading registered instances.
options.feedback: Fortinet states the Manager must be upgraded first for both content and software updates.

questions.prompt: What happens when a user belongs to more than 150 Entra ID groups?

options.text: FortiSASE cannot retrieve group membership above 150 groups.
options.feedback: The guide documents a 150-group retrieval limit and recommends filtering the SAML group claim.

options.text: FortiSASE automatically creates a local group for every membership.
options.feedback: The documented limitation is retrieval failure, not automatic group creation.

options.text: FortiSASE ignores the user's SAML signature after 150 groups.
options.feedback: The limitation concerns group membership retrieval, not signature validation.

options.text: FortiSASE converts all groups into a single administrator role.
options.feedback: The recommended workaround is to filter relevant groups in Entra ID.

questions.prompt: Why must agent traffic use one stable public IP during SAML login?

options.text: Entra ID signs the assertion using the client's public IP.
options.feedback: The issue is source-IP stability during the SAML transaction, not IP-based signing.

options.text: SAML IdP traffic must retain one stable public IP.
options.feedback: The guide warns that load-balanced egress changing the public IP during the redirect can cause SAML failure.

options.text: FortiSASE uses the public IP as the SAML entity ID.
options.feedback: The entity ID is a configured identifier, not the client's public address.

options.text: The agent tunnel cannot route traffic through more than one ISP.
options.feedback: The constraint is a stable source IP during SAML login, not a blanket ban on multiple ISPs.

questions.prompt: Which certificate choice reduces recurring IdP updates when the default SP certificate renews?

options.text: A self-signed IdP certificate removes the SP certificate requirement.
options.feedback: The SP certificate still participates in the SAML configuration and optional signature verification.

options.text: A short-lived client certificate replaces the IdP signing certificate.
options.feedback: Client certificates do not replace the IdP signing certificate.

options.text: A custom SP certificate avoids frequent IdP certificate updates.
options.feedback: The built-in default certificate periodically renews; using a custom certificate avoids repeated pin updates.

options.text: A FortiClient machine certificate automatically pins the SP certificate.
options.feedback: The SP certificate is configured in the FortiSASE SAML wizard.

questions.prompt: What must align for FortiSASE to map the authenticated user and group?

options.text: Only the Entra application display name must match the FortiSASE tenant.
options.feedback: The display name does not replace SAML attribute mapping.

options.text: Only the FortiClient device name must match the user's email.
options.feedback: The user and group claims are the relevant SAML identity values.

options.text: The IdP certificate subject must equal every group name.
options.feedback: The certificate authenticates the assertion issuer; claims carry user/group information.

options.text: Claim mapping must align username and group names on both sides.
options.feedback: FortiSASE and Entra ID must agree on the claim names and values used for username and groups.

questions.prompt: Which IP protocol number should the SD-WAN service rule match for PIM?

options.text: PIM is matched by IP protocol number 103 in the service rule.
options.feedback: Fortinet's example uses protocol 103 to classify PIM traffic for the SD-WAN service.

options.text: PIM is matched by TCP destination port 103 in the service rule.
options.feedback: PIM is an IP protocol, not TCP port 103.

options.text: PIM is matched by UDP destination port 224 in the service rule.

questions.prompt: What does pim-use-sdwan change for multicast routing?

options.text: It converts every multicast packet into a unicast tunnel.
options.feedback: The option controls PIM's use of SD-WAN, not multicast-to-unicast conversion.

options.text: pim-use-sdwan makes PIM neighbor checks and packets use SD-WAN.
options.feedback: The setting makes PIM use SD-WAN when checking RP neighbors and sending PIM packets.

options.text: It disables PIM and relies only on IGMP snooping.
options.feedback: PIM remains enabled; the setting integrates PIM with SD-WAN path selection.

options.text: It forces the RP to reside on the SD-WAN hub.
options.feedback: The RP address is configured separately; the option controls PIM's SD-WAN use.

questions.prompt: What must be done with ADVPN shortcuts for multicast-steered services?

options.text: Enable shortcuts on every member to accelerate PIM joins.
options.feedback: The documented limitation requires shortcuts to be disabled for the service.

options.text: Move multicast to the implicit rule and keep shortcuts enabled.
options.feedback: That does not address the ADVPN incompatibility.

options.text: Disable ADVPN shortcuts for multicast-steered SD-WAN services by design.
options.feedback: Fortinet states ADVPN is not supported when SD-WAN steers multicast traffic.

options.text: Disable the SLA so shortcuts remain the only path.
options.feedback: The multicast example uses an SLA rule and disables shortcuts.

questions.prompt: A ping SLA is healthy, but multicast receivers still lose streams. What is unproven?

options.text: The FortiGate has no active SD-WAN members.
options.feedback: A healthy SLA indicates that at least one monitored member is reachable.

options.text: The multicast source has stopped sending every packet.
options.feedback: The ping SLA does not establish source behavior either way.

options.text: The firewall policy has automatically allowed multicast traffic.
options.feedback: A health check does not prove multicast policy or PIM state.

options.text: A healthy ping SLA does not prove PIM adjacency.
options.feedback: The probe proves reachability to its target, not RP neighbor state or multicast forwarding.

questions.prompt: An endpoint is absent from an ADOM's Asset Identity List. Which rule has priority?

options.text: Device-specific source rules override broad all-device rules here.
options.feedback: FortiAnalyzer gives individual-device rules precedence over broad all-device rules.

options.text: The global FortiGate log source always overrides every exclusion.
options.feedback: The source rules are per ADOM, and device-specific rules take priority.

options.text: The EMS connector always overrides FortiNAC log identity.
options.feedback: There is no universal source-type priority; the documented rule is device-specific over all devices.

options.text: The most recently created source always overrides every older source.
options.feedback: The guide documents device-specific precedence, not creation-time precedence.

questions.prompt: A central incident is visible, but its Triggering Event tab cannot load. What is the right path?

options.text: Rebuild the Manager PostgreSQL database to recreate raw events.
options.feedback: PostgreSQL stores incident metadata, not the raw event database.

options.text: The Manager fetches raw event data from the originating instance.
options.feedback: Raw events are not stored centrally; the Manager requests them from the instance where the incident occurred.

options.text: Reinstall the Manager license to restore event retention.
options.feedback: Licensing does not change the documented on-demand raw-event architecture.

options.text: Export the incident from FortiAnalyzer and import it manually.
options.feedback: The source FortiSIEM instance is the correct raw-event retrieval target.
